items.title: Bobby Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: I’ve been to Japan twice. I’d say this is the most musical feeling I’ve had, the best musical experience I’ve had for a long time. ... now that I’m doing a lot of recordings with Marty and we have a little group called The Orphan Newsboys

ctx.x: How has Dixieland — this could be a hard question, but we’ll try it — how has Dixieland music changed from, I don’t know, its New Orleans heritage?

Well it’s changed quite a bit. In the old days, I guess in New Orleans in the 1920s and even before that, they called it Dixieland jazz and they had mostly blacks playing that © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

type of music. And now, in the 90s now they have a whole different type of combinations of Dixieland bands. The name “Dixieland” is really a bad term because it puts a label on the type of music that actually was played. Actually it’s called “classic jazz” or “traditional jazz,” that’s what I like to call it. And back in the 20s when they had Johnny Dodds and Louis Armstrong and oh — Jimmy Noone, Mancy Carr, Lillie Delk Christian, Earl Hines, all these different stars in jazz in the 20s, were black artists.
